text: A fathom is six feet of water, the unit sailors used when they lowered a weighted line to find the bottom, and to fathom once meant to measure that depth. The word kept the idea and dropped the water: to fathom something is to get to the bottom of it in your head. You meet it most often in the negative, as in I cannot fathom why he did that. Here the writer means the effect is so plain that barely any economics is needed to work it out.

Skittish means nervous and easily spooked, ready to jump or clam up at the smallest hint of trouble. It began with horses shying at a sudden noise, and it now covers people and even markets, as in investors turned skittish. The tutors here are skittish because their work is illegal and the stranger in the doorway might be an inspector.

To bedevil something is to plague it with trouble that keeps returning, so the thing limps along and never quite works. There is a devil sitting inside the word, and that is the picture it carries: something small and persistent making mischief. Journalists use it for projects and policies that never come right. Here a shortage of money has dogged the 5+2 scheme city by city.

When something is in full swing it is going at its busiest, fully under way rather than just starting or winding down. A party, a season or a school term can all be in full swing. Here the tutoring centre was mid-lesson and mid-transaction when the inspectors walked in.

Evidence is incriminating when it tends to show that someone has committed a crime. The verb behind it, incriminate, is the one in the American right against self-incrimination, the refusal to say anything that could be used to convict you. Here the incriminating evidence is the ordinary paperwork of a tutoring session, which the crackdown has turned into proof of an offence.

To scope something out is to look it over carefully in advance, sizing it up before you act. It comes from scope in the sense of a telescope or a rifle sight, and it stays fairly informal. The investigators scoped out the computer system to see what had been charged and what had been taught.

Services rendered is the set phrase for work actually performed and therefore owed payment, the wording you still see on invoices and bills. Rendered here means given or provided, an old sense of the verb that survives mostly in this phrase. The inspectors were matching what customers had paid against the lessons they had received.

A sting is an operation in which police pose as ordinary customers or criminals to catch people in the act, nothing to do with bees. The word came from confidence tricks, where the sting was the moment the victim was fleeced, and police borrowed it for their own traps. Here the authorities filmed their raid on the tutoring centre and posted the video.

Stirring music is music that rouses strong feeling, the swelling patriotic kind, not music being mixed in a bowl. The verb stir means to move something, and a stirring speech or tune moves you emotionally. The joke is that a raid on a maths tutor was set to music fit for a heroic rescue.

A scourge was originally a whip, and the word now means anything that inflicts widespread suffering: a scourge of famine, of disease, of corruption. Calling something a scourge is strong language, reserved for real menaces. The writer uses it sarcastically, since the dangerous scourge being raided is children studying extra maths.

Heaven forfend is an old-fashioned way of saying heaven forbid, a mock-horrified exclamation at the thought of something happening. Forfend is an archaic verb meaning to ward off or prevent, and it survives almost nowhere else. Writers use it now for comic effect, as here: heaven forbid that children should study even more maths.

To stage an event is to organise and carry it out deliberately, the way you stage a play, a protest or a comeback. It does not mean the thing was fake, though a staged photo is a posed one, so context decides. Here authorities across China have staged raids, meaning they planned and mounted them.

To take a different tack is to try another approach after the first one has not worked. Tack is a sailing word: a boat cannot sail straight into the wind, so it zigzags, and each leg of the zigzag is a tack. Note that it is tack, not tact, which is a separate word meaning sensitivity about what to say.

Naming and shaming is the tactic of publishing the identities of people or firms who have broken rules, so that public embarrassment does the punishing. Governments reach for it when fines are hard to collect or offenders are too numerous to prosecute. In Changsha the authorities released the addresses of 113 tutors.

Illicit means not allowed, either by law or by the rules of a place or profession: illicit drugs, an illicit affair, illicit trade. It sits close to illegal but often carries a whiff of secrecy and disapproval rather than a strict legal judgment. The illicit tutors here are teaching ordinary school subjects for money, which the 2021 rules forbid.

Calligraphy is the art of beautiful handwriting, and in China it is a serious traditional art form taught with brush and ink. It counts as a cultural rather than an academic subject, which is why classes in it are still permitted. That is the point of the disguise: a boy is enrolled in calligraphy on paper and studying maths in the room.

A maths olympiad is a competitive problem-solving contest, running from school level up to the International Mathematical Olympiad, where national teams compete. Success in them long helped Chinese students stand out to selective schools, which is exactly why olympiad coaching is discouraged now. Maths is the British spelling of what Americans call math.

A guidance counsellor in a school is the staff member who advises students on courses, applications and problems at home. Here the title is being borrowed as cover: wealthy families hire a private one whose real job is tutoring. The quotation marks in the article signal that the label is a fiction.

Earnest means sincere and serious in intention, without irony or pretence. It is usually approving, though it can hint at someone trying a little too hard. The writer calls the tutors earnest to underline the oddity of the situation: they are sincere teachers who now count as criminals.

The prefix quasi- means seemingly or almost, so a quasi-criminal underworld is one that resembles a criminal underworld without quite being organised crime. You will meet quasi- often in formal writing, as in a quasi-judicial body or a quasi-governmental agency. It is a useful hedge when something has the shape of a thing but not the full substance.

The underworld is the hidden world of criminals and illegal dealing inside a society, a metaphor borrowed from the ancient Greek underworld of the dead. Saying people have joined an underworld implies networks, secrecy and codes rather than one-off rule-breaking. Here it is used with deliberate irony about parents and maths tutors.

Something deep-seated is firmly established far below the surface and therefore hard to shift: a deep-seated fear, a deep-seated problem. The image is of something seated, or settled, deep inside. The article's point is that policy tends to bounce off social patterns this deep.

Unintended consequences are the effects of an action that its authors did not plan on, and the phrase is a standard one in economics and public policy. They are not always bad, but the term usually flags a rule that produced something close to the opposite of what it intended. Banning tutoring to ease pressure, and thereby creating an expensive secret market, is a textbook case.

Double reduction is the English name for the Chinese policy launched in 2021 that set out to reduce two things at once: the homework schools set and the for-profit tutoring outside school. It is the rule that made most academic tutoring illegal. Chinese policies are often known by a short counting label like this.

A blanket ban is one that covers everything in a category with no exceptions, from the image of a blanket laid over the whole thing. Blanket works the same way in blanket coverage or a blanket rule. The article is careful to say the tutoring restriction is not a blanket ban, since ballet and coding classes are still allowed.

Long-suffering describes someone who has put up with hardship or annoyance patiently for a long time, usually with a touch of sympathy or humour. A long-suffering fan supports a team that never wins. Here it is the students, enduring years of homework.

A for-profit organisation exists to make money for its owners, as opposed to a non-profit, which must put any surplus back into its purpose. The distinction matters in law and tax almost everywhere, and it matters here: China's rules target for-profit tutoring of core subjects, not tutoring as such. Some companies survived by converting to non-profit or non-academic forms.

An entrance exam is a test you must sit to be admitted somewhere, with the places going to the highest scorers. China has two big ones: the zhongkao at about fifteen, which decides your secondary school, and the gaokao at about eighteen, which largely decides your university. Systems like this are meant to be hard to bribe, and they are also why extra preparation is worth so much.

This phrase plays on the military-industrial complex, President Eisenhower's 1961 term for the web of arms firms and officials whose shared interest keeps defence spending high. Swapping in another word is now a standard formula, as in the prison-industrial complex. Here it means the whole moneyed industry that had grown up around exams.

A listed company is one whose shares are traded on a stock exchange, so anyone can buy a piece of it and its price is public every day. Listing raises money for the company and exposes it to the market's daily judgment. New Oriental and TAL were listed in New York, which is how the damage to them could be measured to the dollar.

New Oriental and TAL Education were the two giants of Chinese private tutoring, both listed on American stock exchanges and worth tens of billions of dollars before 2021. The double reduction policy destroyed most of that value almost overnight. Both survive today by teaching adults and non-academic subjects instead.

A cram school is a private school that exists purely to drill students for an exam, cramming in material rather than educating broadly. They are an institution across East Asia, known as juku in Japan and hagwon in South Korea. To cram is to stuff something full, which is what a week of last-minute revision feels like.

A listed company's market value is what all its shares are worth added together, which is the price of one share times the number of shares. It moves every day with the share price, so a firm can lose most of its market value without any cash being taken from it. The 100 billion dollars wiped out here is value investors no longer expect, not money removed from a vault.

To wipe out a sum of money is to destroy it entirely, and in financial writing it usually describes value that has vanished as prices collapse. The image is of wiping a surface clean. Nobody carried the 100 billion dollars away: the shares are simply worth that much less than they were.

In business, to pivot is to change what your company does while keeping the same people and assets, a term that came out of Silicon Valley start-ups. Literally a pivot is the fixed point something turns on, so the idea is a turn rather than a fresh start. The tutoring giants pivoted to adult education when their old business became illegal.

When an activity is pushed underground it carries on in secret, out of sight of the authorities, with no suggestion of being literally below ground. The same image gives us the underground press and underground music, which are outside official channels rather than in a basement. Demand for tutoring did not disappear; it stopped advertising.

A channel here is a route along which something travels, the way a river channel carries water: goods, money, information and, in this case, tutoring all move through channels. New channels means new ways of reaching customers, such as word of mouth and private messaging instead of shopfronts and adverts. It is a very common business and diplomatic use of the word.

Chaguan is the name of The Economist's column on China, and the columnist writes under that name instead of a byline, as this newspaper does with all its columns. The word means teahouse in Chinese, traditionally a place where people met to talk and gossip. So Chaguan visited a cluster of tutoring centres means the columnist did.

Nondescript means so ordinary and featureless that there is nothing to describe, which is why nobody notices it. The word literally says not describable. The tutoring centre sits in a nondescript office tower on purpose, since the whole point is not to be found.

Expressly means explicitly and deliberately, spelled out rather than implied, as in a rule that expressly forbids something. It is the adverb behind an express prohibition, and it has nothing to do with speed. The tutor admitted doing something the rules name outright.

A buoy floats, and something buoyant floats or rises. Economists use it for demand, prices or an economy that stays strong and refuses to sink, and it describes a cheerful mood too. Demand for tutoring is buoyant: squeezing the supply has not pushed it down, so prices went up instead.

To pose as someone is to pretend to be them, taking up a false identity or role. A journalist might pose as a customer, a detective as a buyer. Here the maths lessons are posing as calligraphy, disguised on paper as a permitted subject.

The yuan is the unit of Chinese money, part of the currency officially called the renminbi, which means the people's currency. One US dollar is worth roughly seven yuan, which is how 20,000 yuan comes to nearly 3,000 dollars. Newspapers usually give the dollar equivalent in brackets for exactly that reason.

An arms race is a competition in which each side builds up weapons because the other side is, so everyone spends enormously and nobody ends up safer, as the United States and the Soviet Union did with nuclear weapons. The phrase now covers any contest with that shape. Parents adding French, boxing and gymnastics because other parents have are in an arms race over activities.

A swot is British slang for someone who studies very hard, roughly what an American might call a grind, and to swot is to study intensively. The heading sets it beside SWAT, the police unit, because the two sound identical. The pun is a police-style team raiding studious children.

SWAT stands for Special Weapons And Tactics, the heavily armed American police units sent to hostage situations and armed sieges. The heading's joke is that inspection teams are being sent against tutoring with something of that energy. Both halves of the pun sit in the heading: swot and SWAT.

A tiger parent is a mother or father who pushes a child extremely hard at school and music practice, allowing little else. The term spread after Amy Chua's 2011 book Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother, which described that upbringing in Chinese-American families. The article uses it and then complicates it, since the pressure is not coming only from ambitious parents.

A tinge is a slight trace of a colour, so something tinged with a feeling has a faint streak of it running through. Admiration tinged with jealousy, sadness tinged with relief. Beijingers' contempt for Haidian is tinged with envy: they look down on it and want what it has.

Haidian is the north-western district of Beijing where the country's top universities, including Peking and Tsinghua, and many technology companies sit. Its schools are famous for academic intensity and its families for driving their children hardest. It works in Chinese conversation rather as an American might invoke Palo Alto.

Upward mobility is the movement of a person or family to a higher position in society than the one they were born into, usually through education, work or luck. The whole idea is called social mobility, and it can run downward as well as up. Haidian's rich families are worried about the downward direction.

Slippage is a gradual slipping backwards or falling short: schedule slippage means a project quietly running late. Here downward slippage means a family sliding to a lower rung in society than the one it occupies now. The word suggests a slow, unglamorous loss rather than a sudden fall.

A compelling argument is one you find hard to resist agreeing with, and a compelling film is one you cannot look away from. It comes from compel, to force, but nobody is being forced: the pull is on your attention or your judgment. Mr Gao's explanation is compelling because it is obviously true once said.

The 5+2 model is China's official answer to the tutoring ban: five days of school plus two extra hours at the end of each day, so children stay on campus until parents finish work. The added time was meant for sport, arts and some review. Underfunded, it has often become supervised homework instead.

To devolve into something is to sink or degenerate into a worse state, which makes it close to the opposite of evolve despite the similar shape. A discussion devolves into an argument; a plan devolves into chaos. There is a second, unrelated political sense, to devolve power, meaning to hand authority down to a regional government.

Alas is an old-fashioned word for expressing regret or sorrow about something, the written equivalent of a sigh. It usually introduces an unwelcome truth: alas, there is no easy fix. Here the regret is that the parents' belief in tutoring is perfectly rational, which is what makes it so hard to dislodge.

The grind is the daily slog of dull, exhausting, repetitive work, from grinding grain between stones. Students and workers both talk about the daily grind. The parents pushing their children through it went through the same grind themselves.

A dog-eat-dog situation is ruthlessly competitive, one in which people will harm each other to get ahead. The phrase is deliberately shocking, since even dogs are supposed not to eat each other. A dog-eat-dog job market means far more applicants than there are good jobs.

To spark joy became a catchphrase after the Japanese tidying expert Marie Kondo advised keeping only the possessions that spark joy when you hold them and discarding the rest. It is now used lightly for anything pleasant, or not. Saying the cram schools may not have sparked joy is a dry way of admitting nobody enjoyed them, before the sharper point that at least everyone could get in.

A scofflaw is someone who habitually breaks a law, usually a minor one, without much shame, and the word is built just as it sounds, from scoff, meaning to mock, plus law. It was invented for a competition in 1924 to name people who kept drinking during American Prohibition. The article's closing point is that the tutoring rules have turned ordinary parents into scofflaws.
